Introduction – ETCS

The technical advantages of the European Train Control System (ETCS) as well as its simple implementation as an overlay system have led to the successful establishment of ETCS not just inside, but also outside Europe. Many countries currently rely on this European technology to modernise their rail networks.

The standardised ETCS has been developed in Europe since the 1990s by several manufacturers under the leadership of UNISIG and has been implemented on the European rail network since the early 2000s. The aim is to replace all the previous national signalling or train control systems with a new, uniform and interoperable system. This is intended to facilitate cross-border rail transport within the EU and increase competitiveness compared to road transport.

The advantages of ETCS compared to the earlier systems are obvious: uniform, public standards enable the manufacturer- independent implementation of on-board and trackside equipment. The standardisation of the interfaces and functionalities ensures interoperability.

In addition, ETCS complies with the highest possible safety integrity level (SIL) 4 and is installed on top of any existing signalling or route safety system.

From an economic point of view, the open standard leads to the further opening up of the supplier market and thus to more favourable investment and lifecycle costs, as well as to a long-term guarantee of system availability. ETCS covers the functional scope of all the previous European train control systems, making it suitable for use in all mainline railway areas: for high-speed lines as well as for main lines in passenger and freight traffic or branch lines with lower traffic volumes, where safety is often the primary concern. ETCS is just as suitable for inner-city suburban railway lines with extremely short train times and high passenger volumes. The European Railway Agency (ERA) is responsible for the promotion and further development of the ETCS standard within the EU with the aim of removing any technological barriers to cross-border rail traffic and thus further strengthening rail as an attractive mode of transport for goods and passengers. Based on the aforementioned advantages, ETCS has already been used worldwide in numerous countries since the end of the 2000s.

Extremely short project times of a few months are among the reasons why the European standard is often chosen also outside Europe. For completed ETCS L1 projects, currently maximum operating speeds of up to 300 km/h and signal headways of around four minutes are achieved. In general, speeds of up to 500 km/h can be technically handled by the ETCS L1 system, so it provides enough headroom for many future projects. Also, rough environmental conditions, as they are e.g., in the desert or in tropical areas are handled well by ETCS systems.

The main components placed on the track for ETCS L1 are:

- lineside electronic units (LEU), to translate signals from signal lamps, interlockings or other devices on the track to telegrams,

- balise cables for telegram transfers to balises,

- switchable balises, to transfer situation-specific telegrams to the passing trains and

- fixed balises, to transfer telegrams with static track information to passing trains.

Solution overview

On the track, centrally and de-centrally controlled and centrally diagnosed ETCS Level 1 full supervision system components are installed. An approach with advanced functionality and well trusted, practically interference-free, low latency, absolutely stable and future proof cable bound systems, based on communication via fibre optics will be the base for this ETCS L1 system. The system will allow real time full transparency regarding the current status of all connected ETCS Level 1 elements, as well as data driven analysis of the whole system. This allows the extraction of information, which can be used for expectable maintenance activities, next to a notification system, reducing operational restrictions to an absolute minimum – up to a total elimination of restrictions for the railway operation.

This means, the system allows a reduction of the trackside maintenance effort to the absolute minimum and therefore implies significantly lowering overall operational expenses – also e.g., for human resources.

All these points are combined in a user-friendly environment, where the system gives the user reliably indications regarding actions to take at the point when indeed needed. This allows focussed work for dispatching tasks and having a complex system running in the background controlled easily by its front-end user.

Next to that, the whole ETCS solution is designed flexibly. Even future updates – if any changes to the track or further extensions will be needed – can be done in parallel seamlessly and with very low effort.

  1. Operating principle of ETCS L1

ETCS Level 1 is composed of two main parts:

- The trackside system including LEUs (Lineside Electronic Unit) and Eurobalises (also called balises in this document).

- The On-Board System (OBS not described in this document).

As described in the figure below, the interlocking (IXL) receives the track status. Computing this information, it will set a safe route by commanding among others the signal to the required aspect. The LEU measures the voltage or current (depending on the interface board used) of the signal aspect and sends the appropriate telegram to the Eurobalise. Further technical details to the LEU and each board, please see chapter 5.

Once the train passes the Eurobalises, it will read their messages by sending a certain frequency down to activate the balise, which then sends back the telegram it contains. This information is read and executed by the On-Board Unit (OBU) and will lead to either stopping the train or to moving forward, including new information about the track.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1: ETCS L1 system overview

  1. Eurobalises and possible usage on the track

Two types of Eurobalises exist: 

- Fixed balises: As indicated by their name, the fixed balises contain static information only (e.g. Kilometric Point, Static Speed Profile (SSP), steep gradient…).

- Switchable balises: Are connected to the balise slices to transmit relevant information to the FlexLEU. They could contain static and dynamic information.

Balises are always part of a Balise Group (BG). Per BG a minimum of two balises and a maximum of eight balises exists.

A way to increase the performance of a decentralized ETCS L1 solution is to mount additional balises far upfront the signal. Those additional infill balises provide the train with a movement authority in advance, which can increase the operational performance.

For further details and for a station centralised solution description, please see chapter 5.

System overview

The available ETCS L1 Solutions are as follows:

- FlexLEU (flexible lineside electronic unit) as a decentralised unit, sensing the status of the connected signals and translating them to telegrams to communicate with the passing trains

- SC-FlexLEU (Station Centralised flexible LEU) solution with compact FlexLEUs for a space saving centralised operation and maintenance

- LMD (LEU Management and Diagnosis) with its status view, log functionality and diagnosis, to supervise and manage the FlexLEUs and the SC-FlexLEUs

In the following chapters these products / solutions are described in detail.

ETCS – Track side system

FlexLEU – application

The track-side system consists of data transmission points where data are transmitted to the trains. At each transmission point, based on the given signal aspect detected by the signal adaptation circuit and/or the digital inputs, the current line speed, the static speed of the accessible line section and a location reference are transmitted.

For railway stations, where many signals are located close together, a station centralised FlexLEU can be used to allow agglomeration of the FlexLEUs and to make a central diagnosis function possible.

![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2: Use Case – FlexLEU Decentralised

FlexLEU architecture

The FlexLEU is a highly modular system that consists of a series of modules called slices.

Each slice implements a specific function. By combining a set of slices, a FlexLEU can be tailored to specific customer needs as well as tailored to each signal, point machine and interlocking output, depending on the given situation in the field.

FlexLEU – System

Slice naming convention

**Nomenclature pattern:** **FS-nIT(mIT)**

- FS…FlexSlice

- n, m…number of interfaces

- IT…interface type

The following interface types are foreseen to be used

| **Interface Type** | **Description** |
| --- | --- |
| FS-CPU | Central processor slice, controlling interface and sensing slices |
| C | C-Interface (balise) |
| LCS | Low Current Sensing |
| HCS | High Current Sensing |
E.g.,

- FS-6LCS – slice with 6 low current inputs

The CPU and PSU slice slightly deviates from this notation as there are no number of interfaces specified.

Typical Use Cases

The following shows typical use cases of the FlexLEU. Due to the flexible nature, more scenarios are possible.

Decentralised

Figure 1: Use Case – Decentralised (options)

The FlexLEUs tap into the signal lamp circuits to acquire the current state of the signal. This information is used to calculate which aspect shall be transmitted via the connected balises. The FlexLEUs are clearly assigned to each signal in their internal systems, to have a clear overview for central monitoring.

Each LEU is by default independent without neither any physical nor logical link between each other. In that case, each LEU provides a Movement Authority (MA) up to the next signal. When the train arrives at the next signal, it first needs to pass the balise located in front of this signal to receive further MA information.

A solution to keep MAs updated over further distances is LEU coupling. This feature connects all LEUs with each other and forwards movement authority information from next LEUs to the passing LEUs and therefore also to their connected balises.

With such a coupling, the MA given to the train does not apply only until the next signal as it can be retrieved from more than only one signal. Therefore, instead of having an MA for only one section, the train could get an MA for multiple sections. In other words, the train will have a smooth speed over several sections not having to slow down and accelerate at each signal.

This movement can be smoothened even further, if infill balises are installed on the track.

Station Centralised FlexLEU

The station centralised flexible LEU is a solution with compact FlexLEU components for a space saving centralised operation and maintenance. Various amounts of LEUs – depending on their configuration (quantity and types of slices), are placed in a larger cabinet as shown below as “Station LEU”. This cabinet can be put e.g., in a technical room close to the interlocking. The functionality equals to the decentralised FlexLEU.

- This station-centralized solution is interlocking independent and can be used for all types of mechanical and relay interlockings besides the electronic interlockings without the need of expensive specific data interfaces typically used by fully-centralized solutions. 

- Interconnection of the LEUs: All LEUs mounted inside this cabinet are able to share information (signal aspects, switch positions) with each next LEU. Via this interconnection – which is also called LEU coupling – multi section movement authorities (MAs) can be generated at once.

- Interface not only to signals but also to switches: By combining information about signal aspects and switch positions, route dependent MAs can be set.

Additional benefits:

- No power supply for ETCS L1 equipment outside the building is necessary.

- As the electronic equipment is installed inside the building, environmental conditions are not critical. 

- Having all the equipment installed inside prevents against vandalism.

- Faulty boards can be easily exchanged in the signalling room instead of going on site.

Centrally Monitored

Figure 3: Centrally Monitored

In addition to the decentralised and station centralised installations, a central connection can be used for diagnosis, maintenance and vitality monitoring purposes. The connection to the central LMD (LEU Management and Diagnosis) can be done via fibre optic cables. For further information on LMD, please refer to chapter “Maintenance & Diagnosis”.

Interfaces and Slices

The figure below shows one of many possible slice combinations as well as the corresponding interfaces for signal read outs and telegram generations.

![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 4: FlexLEU Interface Overview

FS-PSU

The FlexLEU Power Supply Unit provides the internal 24 VDC main power supply for all slices. There is an AC and a DC variant available. Two PSU’s can be mounted in parallel to increase the available power. If the FlexLEU is supplied with an external DC power supply, external measures must be implemented to limit the supply voltage of the FlexLEU to 35 V.

FS-CPU

The central processing unit manages the internally connected slices of a FlexLEU. It assures the internal signal communication backed by safety relevant algorithms and hardware design. This ensures the correct translation from the outside coming signals to the correct telegram that is generated in the FlexLEU. In addition, data communication for diagnosis and maintenance purposes is enabled due to its network capabilities.

USB Device interface

This interface is used for setup and diagnosis purposes, it is not intended for operational use.

USB Host interface

The USB Host interface supports the connection of USB memory devices (USB-Stick). It is intended to install, update and configure the FlexLEU e.g., in the field at the track.

Ethernet Interface

The FS-CPU provides two isolated Ethernet (100BASE-TX) interfaces.

These interfaces can be used for vital and maintenance communication: status read outs and forwarding to LMD, updates, configurations of the FlexLEUs.

FS-2C – balise interface

These slices are the interfaces for Euro balises. They are equipped with two (UNISIG Subset-036 conforming) C-interfaces. Measures are implemented, to assure safe operation and the transmission of correct unique telegrams.

FS-6LCS / FS-6HCS

The FS-6xCS slices provide current sensing inputs. The current sensing of the lamp current circuits is realized with two independent and isolated current sensors per input to ensure safe operation. Two variants with different usable current ranges are available. The measurement can be configured for the expected signal frequency to achieve optimum performance.

Switches

For communication, needed for centralised diagnosis and management of the FlexLEUs, fibre optic connectivity via railway certified COTS switches is used.

Environmental conditions and maintenance

The FlexLEU slice cases provide protection according to IP20. The slices can operate in a PD2 environment in a temperature range of -40 °C to 70 °C with short term condensation at an altitude up to 4000 m (with switches – up to 2000 m).

Accordingly, the FlexLEU needs to be installed in cabinet. For indoor application conditions this might be a standard 19-inch installation cabinet. For outdoor application, depending on the surrounding climatic conditions, a cabinet dimensioned to follow the internal conditions of PD2 is especially necessary. Mechanics

The cabinet contains a DIN rail to which specific slice connectors are attached. The number of slice connectors matches the numbers of slices to be used.

A single slice can be removed and re-inserted without the need to remove neighbouring slices.

![](data:image/png;base64,)![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5: FlexLEU slice dimensions

The system is qualified with a generic outdoor cabinet with inner dimensions of 597mm x 397mm x 182mm (H x W x D) for sufficient air volume to fit into operating temperature limits in most of the geographical installation areas. Passive temperature reduction elements are applied on the cabinet for protection against sun radiation. The final cabinet design has to fit the conditions in the desired installation area, ensuring PD2 environment inside.

Operating Modes

The FlexLEU is able to go into four different modes – depending on the needed actions.

Start-Up

The **Start-Up** mode is used to perform start-up checks and to establish communication with the I/O slices. A predefined procedure is performed, to initialise the system and to check the vital state of all connected slices in the system. If all checks are successful, the **Standalone/Decentralised** **Operation Mode** is entered. In any other case the **Maintenance Mode** is entered. An exception is if the check identifies an issue with any slices, which are configured as not mandatory. An **Operation Mode** is still entered.

Standalone/Decentralised Operation Mode

In this setup, standalone (decentralised) mode applies. Even when the FlexLEUs are station centralised, the logics are internally identical to a decentralised solution. The FlexLEU determines its output states with its application data-based rule set.

In this mode, operating system health state is supervised, inputs are evaluated, outputs are evaluated and set. Slice states are supervised, real time diagnosis and data read out is possible, receival of application data and update of telegram data are performed.

If in normal operation mode a failure is detected, the **Error Shutdown** mode is entered. The **Maintenance Mode** can be entered on request via the diagnosis interface. The **Maintenance Mode** is entered automatically if inconsistent slice states are detected.

Maintenance Mode

In this mode, several system software and hardware health checks, communication checks, integrity checks, as well as update checks are and diagnosis data read out can be performed. All slice states are supervised. If in **Maintenance Mode** a failure is detected, the **Error Shutdown** mode is entered. The **Maintenance Mode** can otherwise only be left if all checks are successful and the request to leave it is received via the maintenance interface.

Error Shutdown

In **Error Shutdown** no safe functions are performed and all vital interfaces (communication) are deactivated. This mode is entered if a self-test detects an internal hardware failure. Other issues lead to the activation of the **Maintenance Mode** instead.

All output states are set and held in safe state. This will activate the default telegram of the connected balise (if connected), to ensure safe operation on the track. Diagnosis data read out (download logs), change of application data, software update is possible.

A reboot is triggered, if a request to leave the error shutdown mode is received via the maintenance interface. This allows to recover from error shutdown mode via any maintenance connection.

Maintenance & Diagnosis

Diagnosis Interface

All diagnosis activities can either be performed by direct accessing the WEB GUI of each single FlexLEU individually or by the central LMD service. LMD is an additional service and cannot be included in the FlexLEU itself due to needed performance, capacity and due to its centralised way of work.

Please note that for the solution concerning the required indication of the health status of the FlexLEU, **EITHER** the solution as described in chapter 7.2 and parts of 5.2.3 (LMD), **OR** the solution without LMD – as described in chapter 7.4 (Basic status information for external systems) will be implemented.

LMD – System overview

The LMD (LEU Management and Diagnosis) allows centralized supervision and management of over the network connected FlexLEUs installed along the track and in stations or technical buildings.

Its central service is the collection of status, logging and diagnosis information from FlexLEUs connected directly via ethernet. Only for short distances copper cables shall be used, the recommendation is to always connect via fibre optic. Next to switches, no further network equipment is necessary.

The overall system architecture of the LMD can be split into the communication network for providing the remote equipment connectivity and the central services enabling the remote equipment management and diagnosis.

The central services are basically composed of the following components:

- Remote LEU Manager (RLM): manages the logical connections to FlexLEUs. The entire communication is handled via RLM and its sub-components.

- Diagnosis and Management Console (DMC) provides a user interface for an operator of the LMD system for supervising and managing FlexLEUs. An administration interface for configuring the LMDs central services is also provided in the context of DMC.

- The DB services provide storage of collected status and diagnosis information from the connected FlexLEUs as well as operational data.

Each equipment configured and integrated in the system can be managed regarding status and diagnosis, as well as regarding software and firmware updates.

LMD – Remote Diagnosis

The status of the registered remote equipment is checked and the information is given to the user of the LMD in real time:

For the FlexLEU the following is shown on the GUI of LMD:

- Status of the FlexLEU (summary)

- Status of the components (FS-CPU, FS-2C, …)

- Status of the interfaces (C, …)

The FlexLEU status is permanently stored in the datastore in logs. For certain events, a notification to the operator on the GUI is issued. Via the GUI, also logs can be observed and downloaded.

LMD – Web GUI (DMC)

The DMC GUI offers functionality to present the current status and diagnosis data for the supervised FlexLEUs. Additionally, the DMC GUI also offers additional functionality to confirm received notifications (if a supervised equipment changed their status to error) or to export the stored data.

Several users can be registered with their own login to the DMC GUI.

- System vitality monitoring (Administrator only):

In addition, the administrator of the system will have access to an application which offers possibilities for the administrator to check the whole system in detail, check if all services are running, to read out the logs of the services, and to check the current status of the connected remote equipment.

The LMD and FlexLEU system will be compliant to cyber security needs based on „IEC 62443“.

**Maintenance:**

The impact of maintenance on railway operations differs between the several components of the system. During maintenance activities on each FlexLEU (SW update, HW exchange, …), railway operations are not possible in the concerned area and the components cannot be under voltage.

The FlexLEU, which is being updated is marked as not in operation on the LMD. In general, depending on the operating mode, the status is shown in the LMD GUI.

FlexLEU – Web GUI

Each FlexLEU has also the ability to be accessed as a single entity individually via a Web GUI via an internet browser. For the general overview and maintenance of all FlexLEUs connected at one glance, please see the description of the LMD.

In this FlexLEU GUI, the user is able to manage slice replacement, software updates, application data installation (only) for each FlexLEU individually.

FlexLEU – Basic status information (for external systems)

As an option, an adaptation of the Web API can be developed by Hitachi Rail, to provide the following relevant basic health status information for external monitoring systems:

1. LEU Id – unique ID that is configured for each FlexLEU

2. Serial number – a unique serial number for each FlexLEU CPU slice

3. Mode – indicating the current operation mode of the FlexLEU

This information can be fetched from the FlexLEU, implemented and displayed in the external system. For data transfer and implementation into the customers network system, two RJ45 ethernet ports are available per each FS-CPU.

LEU Management and Diagnostic - LMD

The previously mentioned devices can either work as decentral units as very simple solutions in the field. A more sophisticated approach is to connect these ETCS L1 devices to a central point, where status supervision, management, easy issue detection and handling is possible. The LMD allows this centralized supervision and management of over the network connected LEUs installed along the track and in stations or technical buildings.

It gives the user remotely the full overview and precise control of the trackside system, enables remote configuration and software updates as well. Therefore, it significantly reduces the maintenance effort and changes the need of regular time-consuming maintenance check-ups on the track by maintenance staff, to selective on demand maintenance activities. It enables early recognition of issues – even before they have an effect on the railway traffic as well as on demand and quick service. Next to reducing costs and freeing up resources, this keeps downtimes very short, up to avoiding downtimes completely.

Figure 10: ETCS L1 and LMD – all capabilities

Figure 10 shows the whole spectrum of capabilities of the Hitachi Rail ETCS L1 system as a combination of LEUs and the LMD in comparison to ETCS L2 systems. It also depicts the independency of interlocking types and the not required radio network on the track. These capabilities are described more in detail below.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 11: Centralized LMD for an ETCS line

Figure 11 shows a typical line equipped with ETCS L1 LEUs. The LEUs are connected to a data network (typically a fibre optic network ring). Via this connection the central server can access to each single LEU. Three applications can run on this server provide the following functionalities:

1. Remote Diagnosis

2. LEU information coupling

3. Remote Temporary Speed restriction management

These functionalities are described in the following chapters.

  1. Remote Diagnosis and Management

The central service of the LMD is the collection of status, logging and diagnosis information from up to 2000 LEUs connected directly via a secure ethernet connection. All connected LEUs down to their detailed module status level are tracked. This data is then stored in the database and ready to be analysed, if any warning or inconsistency will appear. The controls, warnings and other visuals are presented to the user on an interactive Graphical User Interface (GUI) in real-time. Here, the logs also can be downloaded. Depending on the severity, repetition and quantity of the occurring events, also audio supported pop up alarms will appear. This allows railway operators to run the programme in the background, identify problems efficiently and react quickly to anomalies. In addition, it is possible to forward diagnostic data to existing diagnostic systems via a built-in flexible interface.

The overall system architecture of the LMD can be split into the communication network for providing the remote equipment connectivity and the central services enabling the remote equipment management and diagnosis.

Each compatible equipment connected to the system can be configured and its software and firmware can be updated from a central point or from any authorised point and user along the corresponding IT network.

The central services are basically composed of the following components:

- Remote LEU Manager (RLM): manages the logical connections to LEUs. The entire communication is handled via RLM and its sub-components.

- Diagnosis and Management Console (DMC) provides a user interface for an operator of the LMD system for supervising and managing LEUs. An administration interface for configuring the LMDs central services is also provided in the context of DMC – explained in detail in section 2.4.

- The DB services provide storage of collected status and diagnosis information from the connected LEUs as well as operational data. The LMD offers data storage capacity of approximately three months of operation logs, as a mean common value in its minimum configuration. The possible extension of this capacity is unlimited.

  1. LEU Information Coupling (LIC)

Coupled LEUs can exchange information with each other and pass this on to the train. As a result, multi-section signalling can be achieved via ETCS L1. If, in addition to signalling aspects, the LEU also picks up switch positions, route-dependent signalling can be implemented, which has a much higher performance than conventional block signalling.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 12: Example 4 section MA by coupled LEUs

Figure 12 shows LEUs coupled together. This allows to send multi section movement authorities. Those multi section MAs allows higher line speed than conventional light signals with short block sections. Hitachi realized in Hungary a 3 section MA to increase the line speed from 120km/h - with conventional signalling system – to 180km/h. 

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 13: route dependent MA

As already mentioned in the beginning of this chapter coupling of signal information with the position of the switches can bring further added value. This combination allow route dependent movement authorities.

  1. Remote Temporary Speed Restriction (TSR) management

Slow speed sections can be generated from a central workstation with an accuracy of up to a metre and can then be automatically loaded into the relevant connected LEUs in the field. An authorised person defines the start and end of the required TSR based on predefined TSR zones. Next, the system independently calculates the necessary data and ETCS telegrams and automatically loads them into the LEU after approval by the authorised person. It is also possible to set an activation and deactivation time for the TSR. The function complies with the highest safety standard, Safety Integrity Level 4 (SIL4), and replaces the use of throw balises, which would require the LEU to be adapted to individual construction sites.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 14: online temporary speed restriction management

ETCS infrastructure implementation programme

The typical ETCS L1 implementation programme consists of several milestones. The duration of such an implementation programme depends on several factors and ca vary from 1-3 years.

Those factors ca vary depending on a first project in a country and follow up projects or pure roll out projects. 

When doing the first implementation of an ETCS projects in a courtly or for an infrastructure manager, the initial design of the data preparation rules is time consuming. At this stage the performance output of an ETCS system can vary from high to low performant.

Therefore the design of the data preparation rules is a process with needs continuous cooperation between the system supplier and the operator to tailor the ETCS language to the need of the operator. Hitachi is experienced in that approach and has a long list of lines which were upgraded with ETCS L1 and a higher performance than before.

Topics to be taken into consideration in the design phase of the data preparation rules are:

  - Description of signalling system

  - References where input data can be found

  - Description of level crossings

  - Positions of infill balises

  - Description of interface to trackside with all relevant parameters

  - Description of entry and exit situations

  - Definition of national values

  - Definition of linking

  - Definition of speed and gradient profile

  - Definition of track conditions

  - Description of special operational scenarios (e.g. Call on signal)

Input data needed:

  - Schematic Plans including locations of:

    - Switches

    - Signals

    - Targets of the exit routes and their locations

    - Level crossings (=LX), LX Signals, LX Activation points (if applicable).

    - Platforms

  - Route tables – including all possible routes which need to be considered, also shows if any tracks are not supervised by the interlocking but within the ETCS area

  - Switch table – including position of point and the end of the deviation. Also including maximum valid speed.

  - Gradient profile

  - Speed profile

  - Track condition areas (if applicable) – showing start and end of the track conditions (bridges, tunnels, powerless sections, big metal masses etc.)

  - Country Code and reserved ID’s for the Transmission Points

  - Lamp parameters

  - National Values

After fixing the data preparation rule design phase the data preparation for each LEU and balise can start. In parallel the Hardware is shipped on site and the HW installation can start. 

Further milestones are installation validation, testing of the LEU configuration and operational tests before the national homologation and certification starts.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 21: Typical ETCS L1 implementation milestones

The real duration of an ETCS implementation differs mainly due to the factors:

- First implementation of an ETCS project inside the country (intense brainwork to design the optimal data preparation rules – in this phase the final operational performance is influenced mainly)

- Access to the track: 

  - Installation during without service interruption can lead to short installation cycles during night shifts, or

  - Uninterrupted track access by closing tracks for the installation and testing period.

  - Availability of needed data and track schematics

ETCS Onboard System

Technical description

The ETCS L1 solution on the onboard side consists of several components:

            1. EVC: European Vital Computer which is the core of the system and a 2x2oo2 computer system

            2. BTM+BTM Antenna: Balise Transmission Module which handles the communication with the balises

            3. DMI: Driver Machine Interface

            4. Speaker for acoustic warnings

            5. JRU: Juridical recording unit

            6. Accelerometer (optional) to increase the positioning accuracy of the odometry.

            7. Wheel sensors for speed and distance measurement

            8. CMD: Cold movement detection for ETCS L2 configurations

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The number of equipment dan design of the ETCS system is depending and specific to each vehicle type

ETCS OBS retrofit programme

The typical ETCS OBS retrofit programme is shown on an example from the Asian region:

The OBS main project objective was to deliver and integrate the following:

- one on-board unit (comprising one EVC, one JRU, one BTM Antenna, two wheel sensors, one accelerometer, one radar and two DMIs) for a locomotive unit (Alstom AHK type from 1980).

- two on-board units (where each unit comprises one EVC, one JRU, one BTM Antenna, two wheel sensors, one accelerometer, one radar and one DMI) for a DMU unit (Hitachi THN type from 1983).

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 22: vehicle selection for the on-board integration

**Secondary project objectives:**

- Integration of the DMI into the driver’s desk of the locomotive, requiring significant adaptation due to the age and layout of the cab. 

- Implementation of a service brake interface, in addition to the emergency brake interface. This requirement introduced extra engineering complexity for Hitachi Rail and resulted in a variation order from the customer.

- Installation of the latest ETCS software release, enhancing performance and providing an improved operational experience for the driver.

**Project Context** 

This project is part of a broader national ETCS deployment program initiated by the enduser SRT, aiming to modernize Thailand’s rail network. The introduction of ETCS onboard technology is designed to ensure full compatibility with the new ETCS trackside systems being rolled out across the country by Hitachi Rail GTS and other suppliers.

**Hitachi Rail Scope of Work** 

Hitachi Rail was responsible for the complete lifecycle of the onboard integration, including: 

- Overall project management and acting as the technical solution leader 

- Site surveys of the selected vehicles (for onboard installation)

- Endtoend integration design, covering mechanical, electrical, and pneumatic modifications necessary to install the ETCS solution 

- Hardware and software installation, followed by testing and commissioning activities 

- Certification, culminating in delivery of the safety case 

The re-engineering of key subsystems—particularly the pneumatic braking system—required close collaboration between engineering and installation teams. 

**OBS Hardware Component Suppliers** 

- EVC Cabinet (including BTM) → Arnstadt (Germany) 

- OTE BTM Antenna → Thales (Belgium) 

- DMI → Bachleitner (Germany) 

- Wheel Sensors → Hasler (Czech Republic) 

- JRU → Hasler (Czech Republic) 

- Radar → Deuta (Germany)
